Review: The Power of Exponents and Scaling

We seem to be missing quite a few people today, but we can manage. I hope you all enjoyed the activity last time. We’re going to do something even more fun later today, but first, I want us to go over the two-dimensional scaling problem together. I saw a few struggles here and there, so let’s break it down.

I gave you this kind of crazy question: How many sesame seeds can cover the entire classroom floor?

I’m not going for absolute precision here; we’re going for orders of magnitude. Let’s start with the classroom. I was feeling a bit lazy today, so let’s just say this classroom is approximately 10 \text{ meters} by 10 \text{ meters}. One side might be a little longer, one might be a little shorter, so 10 by 10 evens things out.

The area of the classroom, which we’ll call \text{Area}_{\text{CR}}, is pretty straightforward. We multiply the length by the width: \begin{align*} \text{Area}_{\text{CR}} &= 10 \text{ m} \times 10 \text{ m} \\ &= 10^1 \text{ m} \times 10^1 \text{ m} \\ &= 10^2 \text{ m}^2 \end{align*}

Now, we can easily calculate the area of a single sesame seed. A seed is tiny, about 1 \text{ millimeter} by 1 \text{ millimeter}. By this point, you should all know that a millimeter is 10^{-3} meters. So, let’s find the area of the seed: \begin{align*} \text{Area}_{\text{seed}} &= 1 \text{ mm} \times 1 \text{ mm} \\ &= 10^{-3} \text{ m} \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} \\ &= 10^{-3 + (-3)} \text{ m}^2 \\ &= 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2 \end{align*}

I want to pause here because I spotted a few mistakes where folks would add the exponents incorrectly when squaring a unit. When you are squaring a number, whatever you do to the number, you better be doing to the unit as well! And remember, squaring a number means multiplying it by itself. So (10^{-3})^2 is not 10^{-3+2}. It is 10^{-3 \times 2} = 10^{-6}.

If you ever get confused about multiplying exponents, think of it this way. Let’s use the numbers 6 and 7—six and seven are still in vogue, right? If you multiply 10^6 by 10^7, you are just stringing together a bunch of tens. Because you are multiplying, the powers add up: \begin{align*} 10^6 \times 10^7 &= \underbrace{(10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10)}_{6 \text{ times}} \times \underbrace{(10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10)}_{7 \text{ times}} \\ &= 10^{6+7} \\ &= 10^{13} \end{align*}

But if you raise a power to a power, like (10^6)^7, you are taking that whole block of six tens and multiplying it by itself seven times over: \begin{align*} (10^6)^7 &= \underbrace{10^6 \times 10^6 \times 10^6 \times 10^6 \times 10^6 \times 10^6 \times 10^6}_{7 \text{ times}} \\ &= 10^{6 \times 7} \\ &= 10^{42} \end{align*} That is an insanely huge number—42 zeros trailing the one! At this point, I might be beating a dead horse, but this distinction is super important.

If you have a square computer chip that is 10^4 micrometers on each side, what is its total area in square micrometers?

To find the area, you square the side length, which means multiplying 10^4 by itself. Remember our rule for raising a power to a power: (10^4)^2 becomes 10^{4 \times 2}, which equals 10^8 square micrometers. You multiply the exponents here, you don’t add them!

Finally, we can figure out how many of those small seeds fit in the big classroom. We just divide the big area by the small area, making sure our units match: \begin{align*} \text{Number of seeds} &= \frac{\text{Area}_{\text{CR}}}{\text{Area}_{\text{seed}}} \\ &= \frac{10^2 \text{ m}^2}{10^{-6} \text{ m}^2} \\ &= 10^{2 - (-6)} \\ &= 10^8 \end{align*}

That is 100 \text{ million} sesame seeds! It seems like a big number, right? But compared to the technology we deal with every day, it’s nothing. Remember the computer chips we talked about last week? In the area of your fingernail plate, we can squeeze in about 10 \text{ billion} transistors!

What is a Transistor?

Speaking of transistors, let’s switch gears. You can still buy macroscopic transistors if you’re an electronics hobbyist making an anti-burglar alarm or alternating Christmas lights. But what actually is it?

Simply put, a transistor is an electronic switch. You can tell the transistor to either pass electricity through it, or block electricity. It’s a pass/no-pass gate.

Why is this important for computers? Computers are digital, meaning they operate on states of one or zero. If electricity passes through, that’s a “1”. If it’s blocked, that’s a “0”. If you combine enough of these 1s and 0s, you can do just about anything. Eight digits make a letter. Combine those to make words, paragraphs, and novels. You can do math operations—add, subtract, multiply, divide. String enough together, and you get colors, shapes, and videos! Transistors are the lifeblood of our digital world.

The Magic Material: Semiconductors

So, what are these transistors made of? Remember the mystery crystal you played with? It was silicon!

In elementary or middle school, your teachers probably taught you that all materials can be classified into two categories: conductors (like copper, which let electricity flow) and insulators (like rubber or quartz, which block it). But there is actually a middle child: the semiconductor.

Semiconductors, like silicon or germanium, “kinda” conduct electricity. But where they come in really handy is that you can program them. By applying an electrical voltage, you can tell the material to conduct or not conduct. This is called “gating.” You can switch it on or off, just like a light switch.

Why couldn’t we just build a computer’s processor out of an amazing conductor like copper?

Copper is always "on" because it freely lets electricity flow. To process digital information using 1s and 0s, we need to be able to block the current just as easily as we pass it. Semiconductors give us that control, letting us program them to act as switches.

How a Transistor Works: The Faucet Analogy

Let’s look at what a miniaturized transistor actually looks like. It has three terminals sticking out. Three is the magic number—just like one, two, three strikes in baseball. These connections are called the Source, the Gate, and the Drain.

If you’re struggling to visualize this strange device, think of it as a water faucet. A faucet has a source (where water gets pumped in) and a drain (where water comes out). The only way water can flow is if you open the valve or the handle. In a transistor, we do this electrically by applying a signal to the Gate.

If a transistor is acting like a faucet, what part of the faucet represents the Source, and what part represents the Gate?

The Source is like the water pipe feeding into the faucet, providing the supply of water (or in our case, electrical charge). The Gate is like the handle or valve you turn; it controls whether the flow is allowed to pass through to the drain or is stopped in its tracks.

The device is made of two types of semiconductors: p-type (positive) and n-type (negative). When the transistor is “off,” electricity can’t flow across the different types of semiconductors. But when you activate the Gate, you create an artificial channel that lets charge carriers—like electrons or their positively charged evil twins called “holes”—flow from the Source to the Drain.

This specific type of device technically rhymes with the word faucet: it’s called a MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor). It is the bread and butter of what is inside our digital devices.

Teaming Up: CMOS and Computer Chips

One MOSFET can only store one digital bit (on or off). Realistically, you want to string together a whole bunch of them to do complex math. The next step up is to pair two different types of transistors together into what is called CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor).

Complementary means you hook up a p-type transistor and an n-type transistor together. When you listen to the news and a technical expert mentions CMOS, this is what they mean! It is a pair of transistors that allows us to build complicated devices like your smartphone.

What is really supporting our modern way of life is our ability to make these transistors incredibly small. We can cram tens of billions of them onto a single computer chip. Your smartphone probably has tens of billions of transistors in it right now. Without them, we’d be living in the Stone Age along with the dinosaurs. Cars, airplanes, medical devices—they all rely on these tiny electronic switches.

Hands-On: Shrinking Transistors

All right, we’re going to do something fun today. I’m putting you in random groups of four, so say goodbye to your buddies just for today!

In your bags, you have five or six different colors of Play-Doh. (Honestly, we should get Intel and Play-Doh to sponsor us!) First, I want everyone to make their own macroscopic model of a MOSFET transistor, about the size of a computer chip—one centimeter by one centimeter.

Once you have built your first one, here is the real challenge: I want you to make a miniaturized version where everything is shrunk down by a factor of two.

This activity models exactly what the semiconductor industry does—constantly finding ways to shrink these devices so we can pack more computing power into the same area. Put your team’s transistors together on a chip, snap a picture, and send it to me. Thanks for the hard work today, everyone!
